title: Big business tells Labor to get a move on with AI
full_text:
Leaders from Wesfarmers, Telstra and BHP are urging the government to move quickly on artificial intelligence policy, warning Australia could be left behind if roadblocks are introduced or decisions delayed until after Christmas.
Business Council of Australia chief executive Bran Black said fearmongers and those hyping up AI were doing the country a "disservice", as assistant minister Andrew Charlton warned against confusing market volatility in technology stocks with the long-term benefits of AI.
"It's not simply a case of saying, 'well, there are opportunities for us to pursue, and therefore let's make sure we get the settings right'," Black said. "We're concerned that if we don't move with sufficient haste, we will see competitor nations get ahead of Australia, and that will be a significant challenge for us."
A bipartisan parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence chaired by Labor MP Jo Briskey has examined the rapid growth of AI use in Australia, calling on data centre developers and regulators alongside major AI companies to discuss best ways to seize opportunity and mitigate risk.
The committee, which is scheduled to publicly report its findings by the end of November, wrote to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last month and urged the government to invest in data centres as a matter of national interest. The committee also gave its approval to change copyright laws that will make it easier for AI developers to train their models here.
Wesfarmers managing director Rob Scott - who oversees Kmart, Bunnings Warehouse and Officeworks - said AI was critical to his company's ability to compete with large multinationals.
"Australia's productivity challenge is well documented, and AI is one of few levers big enough to make a real difference," Scott said. "As the government reflects on these new technologies, safeguards are appropriate, but it's vital we don't introduce roadblocks or unnecessary complexity because the rest of the world - and all our competitors - are getting on with it."
BHP Australia president Geraldine Slattery said AI was making mining safer and more productive. In Western Australia, BHP is using AI-enabled computer vision to detect large rocks and ore spillages, which has improved the volume produced by 180,000 tonnes per year.
"Scaling the gains from AI is now the big opportunity for Australia, but investment will not move faster than certainty about the rules," Slattery said.
Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady said Australia could be more than just a consumer of AI. "Much of the region's AI infrastructure is still to be built, and the countries that move early will reap the biggest reward," she said. "Clear, settled rules, delivered quickly, give investors the confidence to commit."
Technology giants such as Microsoft, Google and Meta and AI factories such as Iren and Coreweave have experienced significant share price volatility over the past month amid concerns about the cost of capital, rising bond yields and widespread cynicism about AI valuations.
Opposition to data centre development also played a key role in the Democrats' clean sweep at the US midterms.
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said on Thursday (AEDT) she expected building new data centres in the US would become "very challenging" as a result.
Charlton used a speech at the ACTU Superannuation Summit in Melbourne on Thursday to calm investor nerves.
"Recent volatility in financial markets has led some to question the durability of the AI boom," he said. "But we need to distinguish between the economic value of AI as a technology and the market valuation of AI companies.
"Investors are rightly asking tougher questions about returns ... but a correction in share prices is not a correction in technological progress."
Nine Entertainment Co.
